newsitem.title: GERMANY: INTERVIEW-DIW says Germany meets Maastricht spirit.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-DIW says Germany meets Maastricht spirit.

text.p: Germany will meet entry criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) by complying with the "spirit" of the Maastricht Treaty, but should be cautious about opening the door to creative accounting measures, according to a leading German economist.

"The spirit of the treaty is definitely met by Germany. I am sure Germany will meet the EMU criteria in the sense that the Treaty has given," Heiner Flassbeck, chief economist at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW) told Reuters in an interview.

But Flassbeck criticised recently-announced plans by the German government to revalue Bundesbank currency and gold reserves to nearer market values, saying that while the idea itself was not economically dangerous, the timing and impression of the government given by the plan was unfortunate.
"It may be necessary, but it is not a good idea to connect it directly with the need to meet the Maastricht criteria. It opens up the discussion about creative accounting," he said.

Germany has been the most prominent and vocal opposer to any "creative accounting" moves made by other European Union governments trying to reduce debt and deficit levels to qualify for Europe's single currency, due to start in 1999.
"Right now, in close connection will a fall in tax revenues, to talk about revaluation of gold stocks and such things was not a very intelligent solution by the German government," Flassbeck said.
"It is reasonable to harmonise the evaluation of gold reserves within the EU, but to open the debate on Thursday was not a very credible policy."

After tax estimates for 1997 showed an 18 billion mark shortfall, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said last Thursday that he planned to revalue the Bundesbank's reserves to closer to market levels.
The move was widely seen as a last ditch attempt to boost government coffers to help Germany meet the Maastricht deficit and debt entry criteria for EMU.
Some independent analysts said Germany was indulging in 'fudging' in a bid to bring its deficit below the 3.0 percent of gross dometic product (GDP) target level.

Economically, however, Flassbeck said Waigel's move to revalue central bank reserves was "not a problem", saying that repricing gold at nearer market levels would not add to price pressure in the wider economy, as some analysts fear.
Flassbeck also said the use of various accounting tricks by EU countries fighting to get into the first round of EMU would not harm the euro as a currency in the longer term.
"All these tricks will be forgotten in half a year after the euro has started its life," he said. "There will be no problem with the strength of the euro."
The DIW economist said the highest probability was that a large group of countries -- as many as 10 or 11 -- will be in the first EMU wave in 1999.

Despite speculation about who will and who won't meet the Maatricht entry rules, Flassbeck said there was "no doubt that there is a large degree of convergence" between European economies, adding that delay to the single curency project was "not a realistic alternative."

He said the question of whether Italy wouuld be among the EMU starters was "a critical point" but said that even if it were not a founding member, he expected it to have a special status within the EMS2 currency grid, giving it effective currency union with the first euro nations.
